name: 4-n-Butylresorcinol
lead: 4-n-Butylresorcinol (also called butylresorcinol or rucinol) is a synthetic resorcinol derivative used in topical serums and creams aimed at hyperpigmentation such as melasma and age spots. It acts as a tyrosinase inhibitor [1][2].

Unlike many other tyrosinase inhibitors, it has been tested in several small randomized human trials in melasma and other pigmentation, with reported improvements versus vehicle [3][4][8][9]. These trials are small and short, and independent comparisons with other agents are limited.

paras: A 2005 study in a mouse melanocyte line found that 4-n-butylresorcinol inhibited melanin synthesis in a concentration-dependent manner and inhibited tyrosinase, the rate-limiting melanogenic enzyme [2]. Reports have also described inhibition of tyrosinase-related protein-1, and a 2017 study reported enhanced proteolytic degradation of tyrosinase in B16F10 melanoma cells [4][10]. A 2013 paper described it as a highly effective tyrosinase inhibitor and noted that many other tyrosinase inhibitors lack clinical efficacy [1].

A 2007 randomized controlled trial evaluated a rucinol serum in patients with melasma [3]. A 2010 randomized split-face trial tested liposome-encapsulated 4-n-butylresorcinol 0.1% cream for melasma, with the same design reported in two journals [4][9]. A 2016 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested a dissolving microneedle patch containing 4-n-butylresorcinol for depigmentation [8].

A secondary summary (an AI-generated encyclopedia page, which carries errors) lists the trial results as improvements in pigmentation and melanin index versus vehicle in studies of about 12 to 52 participants and describes a cited systematic review reporting reductions between 5% and 56% across three studies, with calls for head-to-head comparisons; these figures should be checked against the primary papers [11].

A 2015 paper described a screening method to separate phenolic whitening tyrosinase inhibitors from phenols that induce leukoderma [5]. The AI-generated summary states that the compound is permitted as a cosmetic in the EU, is a quasi-drug whitening agent in Japan, and is reported as minimally irritating at 0.3%, with some internal inconsistencies [11].
Studies have examined dissolving microneedle patches used with serum to enhance transdermal delivery of 4-n-butylresorcinol [6][8].

card.summary: A tyrosinase inhibitor used in melasma and dark-spot serums, with several small randomized trials reporting improvement.
card.note: Trials are small and short; head-to-head comparisons are limited.

quick.overview:
4-n-Butylresorcinol is a lab-made ingredient found in serums for melasma and dark spots.

Several small randomized trials, including split-face and vehicle-controlled designs, have reported pigment improvement, though sample sizes are modest.
quick.mechanism: It inhibits tyrosinase and has been reported to affect tyrosinase-related protein-1, reducing melanin production in cells.
quick.risks: Reports in the sources describe minimal irritation at studied concentrations; regulation varies by country, and figures from secondary summaries should be verified.
